bib.title: Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship, Chapter 2: Meaningful Names

question: What simple rules produce names for variables, functions, classes and packages that a reader can understand without extra context?
contributions: A list of naming rules, each with a before/after code example: intention-revealing, no disinformation, meaningful distinctions, pronounceable, searchable, no encodings, no mental mapping, class and method naming conventions, no cuteness, one word per concept, no puns, solution-domain and problem-domain names, meaningful but not gratuitous context.

results.claim: A name that needs a comment does not reveal its intent; a name should say why it exists, what it does and how it is used.
results.setup: Rule 'Use Intention-Revealing Names'; illustrated with `int d; // elapsed time in days` renamed to elapsedTimeInDays, daysSinceCreation, fileAgeInDays.
results.quote:
If a name requires a com-
ment, then the name does not reveal its intent.

results.claim: Renaming alone makes minesweeper code explicit while operators, constants and nesting stay identical; replacing the int array by a Cell class with isFlagged() hides the magic number 4.
results.setup: getThem() with theList, x[0] == 4, list1 becomes getFlaggedCells() with gameBoard, cell[STATUS_VALUE] == FLAGGED, then Cell.isFlagged(). Java, minesweeper board.
results.quote: Notice that the simplicity of the code has not changed.

results.claim: The problem with unreadable simple code is 'implicity': the degree to which context is not explicit in the code itself.
results.setup: getThem() example; four unanswered questions: what is in theList, what the zeroth subscript means, what 4 means, how to use the returned list.
results.quote: The problem isn’t the simplicity of the code but the implicity of the code
results.note: Apostrophe in the source is a typographic one.

results.claim: Do not name a container accountList unless it is actually a List, and avoid names that are Unix platform names (hp, aix, sco).
results.setup: Rule 'Avoid Disinformation'; footnote 1 adds that even if it is a List, encoding the container type is probably worse.
results.quote: Do not refer to a grouping of accounts as an accountList unless it’s actually a List.

results.claim: Number-series names (a1, a2) are noninformative and noise words (Info, Data, variable, table) add no distinction; names that must differ should mean something different.
results.setup: Rule 'Make Meaningful Distinctions'; copyChars(a1, a2) vs source/destination; Product vs ProductInfo vs ProductData; getActiveAccount / getActiveAccounts / getActiveAccountInfo.
results.quote: If names must be different, then they should also mean something different.

results.claim: Unpronounceable names make code hard to discuss; genymdhms becomes generationTimestamp.
results.setup: Rule 'Use Pronounceable Names'; anecdote about a company's genymdhms; DtaRcrd102 vs Customer.
results.quote: If you can’t pronounce it, you can’t discuss it without sounding like an idiot.

results.claim: Single-letter names and bare numeric constants are hard to search for; a named constant such as WORK_DAYS_PER_WEEK is easier to find than every use of 5.
results.setup: Rule 'Use Searchable Names'; loop `for (int j=0; j<34; j++) { s += (t[j]*4)/5; }` rewritten with NUMBER_OF_TASKS, realDaysPerIdealDay, WORK_DAYS_PER_WEEK.
results.quote:
In this regard, longer names trump shorter
names, and any searchable name trumps a constant in code.

results.claim: Name length should correspond to scope size; single-letter names only as locals in short methods.
results.setup: Author's stated personal preference, cross-referenced to heuristic [N5].
results.quote:
My personal preference is that single-letter names can ONLY be used as local vari-
ables inside short methods.

results.claim: Type and scope encodings (Hungarian Notation, m_ prefixes, I-prefixed interfaces) are impediments in modern typed languages with IDEs; if one must be encoded, encode the implementation (ShapeFactoryImp) not the interface.
results.setup: Rule 'Avoid Encodings', Java; example PhoneNumber phoneString whose name was not changed when the type changed.
results.quote: So nowadays HN and other forms of type encoding are simply impediments.

results.claim: Readers should not have to mentally translate names; single-letter names are placeholders, except loop counters i, j, k with tiny scope (never l).
results.quote:
One difference between a smart programmer and a professional programmer is that
the professional understands that clarity is king.

results.claim: Class names are nouns and avoid Manager, Processor, Data, Info; method names are verbs; accessors, mutators and predicates use get, set, is; overloaded constructors are better replaced by static factory methods with descriptive names.
results.setup: Java, javabean standard; Complex.FromRealNumber(23.0) preferred to new Complex(23.0), with constructors made private to enforce it.
results.quote: Methods should have verb or verb phrase names like postPayment, deletePage, or save.

results.claim: Choose clarity over cleverness or slang in names (DeleteItems over HolyHandGrenade, kill over whack).
Use one word per concept (not fetch, retrieve and get as equivalents) and do not reuse a word for two meanings (add vs insert/append).
results.setup: Rules 'Pick One Word per Concept' and 'Don't Pun'; argument rests on IDE completion lists not showing comments.
results.quote: A consistent lexicon is a great boon to the programmers who must use your code.

results.claim: Names should come from the solution domain (CS, pattern, math terms) first, and from the problem domain when no programmer term exists.
results.setup: Rules 'Use Solution Domain Names' and 'Use Problem Domain Names'; AccountVisitor, JobQueue as examples.
results.quote:
When there is no “programmer-eese” for what you’re doing, use the name from the prob-
lem domain.

results.claim: Variables that belong together get context from an enclosing class (Address, GuessStatisticsMessage) rather than from prefixes; the better context also lets a long function be split into small ones.
results.setup: Listing 2-1 printGuessStatistics (number, verb, pluralModifier locals) refactored in Listing 2-2 to class GuessStatisticsMessage with thereAreNoLetters, thereIsOneLetter, thereAreManyLetters.
results.quote:
Of
course, a better solution is to create a class named Address.

results.claim: Prefixing every class with an application tag (GSD) is gratuitous context; in GSDAccountAddress ten of 17 characters are redundant or irrelevant.
results.setup: Imaginary 'Gas Station Deluxe' app; GSDAccountAddress reused for a customer contact application.
results.quote:
Ten of
17 characters are redundant or irrelevant.

results.claim: Shorter names are better than longer ones if clear; add no more context than necessary.
results.setup: Rule 'Don't Add Gratuitous Context'; Address is fine for a class, accountAddress and customerAddress are fine as instance names.
results.quote:
Add no
more context to a name than is necessary.

results.claim: Do not fear renaming; use refactoring tools and rename when a better name appears.
results.quote: We do not share that fear and ﬁnd that we are actually grateful when names change

limits: No empirical evidence: every rule is the authors' experience and preference, with constructed before/after examples; no study, count or measurement supports any claim.
Examples are Java and C++ era (2008): Hungarian Notation, m_ prefixes, I-prefixed interfaces, javabean get/set and IDE completion arguments reflect that tooling; Python conventions (PEP 8) differ.
The chapter itself says naming depends on descriptive skill and shared cultural background and is hard to teach.
Preferences are flagged as personal (single-letter names only in short methods; footnote 3 says the author gave up the a/the prefix habit).
The chapter byline is Tim Ottinger, though the book is credited to Robert C. Martin.
practices: Choose names that say why a thing exists, what it does and how it is used, including the unit (p.18).
Rename magic values and index positions into named constants or a small class with an intention-revealing method such as isFlagged (pp.18-19).
Do not encode a container type into a name (accountList) and avoid names that collide with well-known terms (p.19).
Do not distinguish names with number series or noise words such as Info, Data, variable, table (pp.20-21).
Make names pronounceable so they can be spoken in discussion (pp.21-22).
Use searchable names; make name length proportional to scope; single-letter names only for short local scopes (pp.22-23).
Drop Hungarian Notation, member prefixes and interface I-prefixes (pp.23-24).
Do not make readers map your names onto other names; loop counters i, j, k are the exception (p.25).
Name classes with nouns, methods with verbs, use get/set/is for accessors and predicates, and prefer named static factory methods to overloaded constructors (p.25).
Choose clarity over humor or slang in names (p.26).
Use one word per concept and never one word for two concepts (pp.26-27).
Prefer solution-domain terms, then problem-domain terms (p.27).
Give names context through well-named classes, functions or namespaces; prefixes only as a last resort; add no gratuitous context (pp.27-30).
Rename when you find a better name and use refactoring tools (p.30).

terms.definition: the degree to which the context is not explicit in the code itself
leaving false clues that obscure the meaning of code, e.g. words whose entrenched meanings vary from the intended meaning
redundant words such as Info, Data, a, an, the that make names different without making them mean anything different
using the same term for two different ideas
encoding type information into the name, from the era of the Windows C API when compilers did not check types
